newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Labour pledges more interventionist stance.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Labour pledges more interventionist stance.

text.p: New Zealand Labour leader Helen Clark said the party would run a more active and interventionist policy than the current conservative government if it won the October 12 general election.
Clark said Labour policy would complement the role of Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash in fighing inflation.
"It's not enough to try and fight inflation by giving Dr Brash a very narrow target range and saying 'go to it'," Clark said in a Sunday night television interview.
"We as a government have to actively intervene to ensure that the investment goes into the skills area, into infrastructure, into low income housing and so on, to act against inflation."
Clark said Labour stood for a "much more active" form of economic management than the current National Party conservative government.

"We are not prepared to say to Don Brash inflation is your problem' and then doing everything to trip him up by creating skills shortages, infrastructure problems, huge demand in the housing market through unplanned immigration surges and huge
increases in user pays pushing inflation up as well."

Labour wants to widen the central bank's target range for underlying inflation from 0-2 percent to minus one to three percent. Unlike New Zealand First and the Alliance, it does not support setting other objectives for the bank such as sustainable economic growth,

"What we would argue is that by widening the target range and deploying a range of other anti-inflationary policies at government level we can get sustainable economic growth. I don't think it's sensible to broaden the Reserve Bank's focus too much, or you lose focus altogether," Clark said.

Clark said Labour did not dispute there had been economic recovery. "The key dispute is over, firstly getting a sustainable rate of growth which is higher than the present, but also making sure that the fruits of growth come down to the ordinary person and their community."
She said she believed four percent growth was sustainable, but this required investment in skills and infrastructure.
Clark reiterated that Labour would not form a coalition with National after the election, and this was an "absolute position".
She said the role of economic nationalist New Zealand First would be pivotal. "Both parties (Labour and National) need New Zealand First. That is the reality."

NZ First, under a coalition with Labour, would be free to seek to introduce legislation to buy back state-owned Forestry Corporation or adopt compulsory superannuation, but Labour would not support these measures.
Clark said New Zealand First, under the influence of strategist Michael Laws, had shifted towards more centrist and orthodox economic positions in some areas.
